items.title: 33 Years Later, the Coldest Quote in Action Thriller History Still Hits Hard
items.summary: The Fugitive took the world by storm when it was released in 1993. Not only was this action-thriller film, based on the television series from the 1960s, a massive box-office success, but it was also a critical darling and, miraculously, a major Oscar contender, receiving nominations for Best Picture and a win for Tommy Lee Jones for Best Supporting Actor. Starring Harrison Ford as Dr. Richard Kimble, a man wrongfully convicted of the murder of his wife who goes on the run from U.S. Marshals, The Fugitive , directed by Andrew Davis , shares little resemblance to other movies recognized by the Academy Awards, even the other blockbusters. And that especially applies to Jones' surprising Oscar win for playing U.S. Marshal Samuel Gerard, who leads the charge in pursuit of Kimble. When voters heard Gerard's legendary line, "I don't care," one of the coldest lines in thriller movie history, they had no choice but to hand Jones the Oscar.
items.t: 33 Years Later, the Coldest Quote in Action Thriller History Still Hits Hard

items.title: Anya Taylor-Joy’s 93-Minute Crime Thriller 'Thoroughbreds' Is the Perfect Watch Before It’s Cut From Streaming
items.summary: One of the most unsung releases of the last decade was 2017’s Thoroughbreds , a thriller deep in the film noir mode with three great actors going toe to toe. With Anya Taylor-Joy , Olivia Cooke , and Anton Yelchin as the architects and participants of a murder plot, it’s less a crime movie and more of a character study, with director Cory Finley mining both pathos and extremely dark comedy from the premise. In an era where minimal-location movies about the sociopathy of the rich were frequently successful discourse machines (including Taylor-Joy’s 2022 vehicle The Menu ), Thoroughbreds was a classically amoral story of kids whose wealth insulates them from consequences, yet you still root for them. The movie was unfortunately ahead of the curve with its note-perfect plotting and criminal ideation, as well as its cast.
items.t: Anya Taylor-Joy’s 93-Minute Crime Thriller 'Thoroughbreds' Is the Perfect Watch Before It’s Cut From Streaming

items.title: 'Star Trek: Deep Space Nine’s Greatest Quote Still Hasn't Been Beaten
items.summary: Star Trek: Deep Space Nine is the black sheep of the Star Trek franchise, a truth that has divided opinions ever since its debut in 1993. It eschews the utopian future that was Gene Roddenberry 's vision, with its enlightenment, moral fortitude, and the wonder of exploration, summed up in the "to boldly go where no man has gone before" phrase from its iconic opening narration. In its place is a gritty, darker series that takes place on a stationary outpost, where the ideal is constantly tested by moral ambiguity, subterfuge, and conflict. Nowhere is that challenge more evident than in Star Trek: Deep Space Nine 's greatest quote, one made 33 years ago that began as a statement of belief in moral righteousness, only to become one of dark irony as the series progresses .

items.title: You Can See Everything overtly riffs on Vertigo. But how big is its debt to Kiarostami’s Close-Up?
items.summary:
The Iranian film-maker’s 1990 tale of impersonation and deception happens to be a favourite movie of the Elizabeth Holmes docufiction’s co-director Lance Oppenheim
• NB: This article contains spoilers

You’re probably sick of hearing how You Can See Everything, about the disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, is the buzziest, coolest, 100% freshest film of the year, but coming out of the screening last week, I couldn’t help but wonder whether Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim had been watching a lot of 90s Iranian cinema. And one film in particular: Close-Up, by Abbas Kiarostami.

If it feels as if You Can See Everything blends truth, lies, fiction and documentary in mind-bending new ways until you’re no longer sure what the hell you’re watching, then Kiarostami, who died in 2016, practically invented this mode 36 years ago. The context could not be more different – analogue 90s Tehran rather than tech-drunk 2020s California – but the themes are the same: Close-Up is a strange story of impersonation, deception and performance, made even stranger by the film-maker’s deliberate meddling.

Continue reading...
items.t: You Can See Everything overtly riffs on Vertigo. But how big is its debt to Kiarostami’s Close-Up?

items.title: Jesse Eisenberg says his films contain ‘no sexuality’. But maybe his fans are just less desperate?
items.summary:
The actor-director has said people don’t interrupt his daytime writing in a public library because he’s not perceived as fanciable. Might that have more to do with the library than with him?

The imminent arrival of Jesse Eisenberg’s new film The Debut should be cause for celebration. Not necessarily because it is good – although its star Julianne Moore seems locked into an Oscar nomination at minimum – but because it means that Jesse Eisenberg has to do press for it. This is always a treat.

While the bulk of big magazine profiles about film people involve journalists breaking their spines to make the subject sound funnier or more profound than they really are, that is never particularly necessary with Eisenberg, because he appears to be a genuine oddball.

Gérard Depardieu has been ordered to stand trial on a charge of raping a female actor at his Paris home in 2018, after an appeals ⁠court rejected his attempt to avoid having the case tried.

The film star, 77, had appealed last year against an investigating magistrate’s ruling that he should stand criminal trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting Charlotte Arnould on two occasions, but judges said on Thursday proceedings should go ahead.

items.title: Amanda Seyfried needed ‘five-factor authentication’ to read You Can See Everything script but still ‘told everyone’
items.summary:

Amanda Seyfried says that the script and footage of You Can See Everything was kept secret even from her until the last possible moment, and that despite being asked not to reveal her involvement in the project she “told a lot of people”.

Seyfried was speaking on the Jimmy Fallon Show on Tuesday, after the film’s extraordinary commercial success in North America, where it is already the third most successful documentary in box office history. Having already played You Can See Everything’s central figure, Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes, in the dramatised TV series The Dropout, Seyfried was called in by directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim to stand in for Holmes after the latter started her prison term in 2023.

items.title: ‘I was very aggressive. They threw me out of every school’ … Julie Delpy on acting, anger and predatory directors
items.summary:
Thirty years after the roles that made her famous, the star of Three Colours: White and the Before trilogy is busier than ever – as a screenwriter and director. But, she says, a lot of people have tried to keep her down

To listen to Julie Delpy talk about her workload is to feel the need for a nap coming on. She is writing six screenplays at the moment that range from dark comedies to thrillers. “I don’t do monoculture,” she says. If her producer hadn’t reined her in, she would be working on five horror film scripts too.

The actor, writer and director says she doesn’t sleep well – she can sit at her desk for up to 18 hours, writing “until I run out of steam. I know you could think I’m exaggerating. I’m not. If you look at my computer, you will see how bad it is.”

We’re on a video call, Delpy from her home in Los Angeles. She is charming – intense and funny in big black-framed glasses. “I look so weird with this angle on my hair,” she says, of the ceiling light behind her. “Like an angry bald man!”

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘I was very aggressive. They threw me out of every school’ … Julie Delpy on acting, anger and predatory directors

items.title: ‘She was so not regretful about killing her husband’: the Iranian film that shines a light on blood money and retributive justice
items.summary:
The co-director of An Eye for an Eye, Tanaz Eshaghian, reveals how she came to make a documentary about a woman facing the threat of execution from her husband’s family – as sanctioned by sharia law

“Even though I was raised here,” says the Iranian-American film-maker Tanaz Eshaghian from her home in New York, “I was brought up with the understanding that there are things that you do and things that you don’t do.” Take her 2006 autobiographical feature, Love Iranian-American Style, about her experience of dating in her 20s, which was, she says, “about how I was supposed to marry a nice Iranian man and stay a virgin”. But by the time she’d graduated from Brown University in Rhode Island “that ship had sailed”, she laughs.

Since Love Iranian-American Style, she has made equally taboo-breaking documentaries about a women’s prison in Afghanistan (Love Crimes of Kabul, 2011), trans people in Iran (Be Like Others, 2008) and disabled teenagers in Pakistan (As Far As They Can Run, 2022). And with each new project, the duality of her heritage (Eshaghian emigrated to the US not long after the Iranian revolution when she was six) has spurred her to focus eastwards, closer to where she was born. “When you’ve been raised in the west you can see how similar the thinking is,” Eshaghian says of the similarities she’s found there: “the conservative thinking, the place of women, what’s allowed, what’s important”.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘She was so not regretful about killing her husband’: the Iranian film that shines a light on blood money and retributive justice

items.title: You Can See Everything passes $100m at global box office as UK release starts strong
items.summary:
The documentary from Nathan Fielder following fraudster Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks leading up to her imprisonment has broken box office records in the UK

Elizabeth Holmes film You Can See Everything has crossed the $100m mark at the global box office as it recorded the highest ever opening weekend figure for a non-music documentary in the UK.

Directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, You Can See Everything earned an estimated $2.5m over the weekend on its sixth week of release in North America, according to Box Office Mojo, bringing its total there to $93.5m. This has been augmented by successful releases in a number of international territories, which has added an estimated $9m for a total of $102.5m.

Continue reading...
items.t: You Can See Everything passes $100m at global box office as UK release starts strong
